insights.title: Middle East conflict becomes the main drag
insights.summary: The Q4 2025 call (T1) did not discuss Middle East conflict risk. In the Q1 2026 call (T2) it became the largest guidance headwind, estimated at 100 to 125 bps of full-year global RevPAR growth. By Q2 2026 (T3), management reported Middle East RevPAR down 43% for the quarter. They also linked the region to construction delays that pushed net rooms growth toward the low end of guidance. Management noted the region is 3% of open rooms and 7% of pipeline rooms.
insights.uw_relevance: This is a new geopolitical exposure that now affects RevPAR, IMFs and unit growth guidance. Disclosures about how far conflict impacts are reflected in forward guidance may be scrutinised if results fall short.

evidence.snippet: Our guidance assumes the conflict in the Middle East could impact full year global RevPAR growth by 100 to 125 basis points.
As a reminder, the Middle East accounts for 3% of open rooms, 7% of pipeline rooms and for full year 2025, 3% of global gross speeds.
Middle East RevPAR declined 43% in the quarter, a bit better than prior expectations on better-than-expected domestic leisure demand.

insights.title: Net rooms growth guidance softens to low end
insights.summary: Net rooms growth language weakened across the three calls. In T1, management said growth was expected to 'accelerate' to 4.5%–5% and the departing CFO said they were 'very comfortable' with it. In T2, management 'still feel comfortable' but began pointing to multiyear CAGR as more instructive. In T3, full-year 2026 growth is 'more likely to be towards the low end', and management again leaned on a 30-month CAGR of 5.2%.
insights.uw_relevance: Unit growth is a core KPI that management highlights to investors. A shift from confident point guidance to defending a multiyear CAGR is a guidance-credibility signal to track.

evidence.snippet: For the full year 2026, net room growth is expected to accelerate up to 4.5% to 5%.

insights.title: Owner relations turn guarded after owner letter
insights.summary: In T1, the CEO discussed franchisee economics openly as a recovery issue. By T3, an analyst referred to an owner letter, and the CEO declined to give an official response. He also gave only a non-specific answer on how much owner concessions would hit Marriott's P&L. Over the same period, management introduced concessions: loyalty charge-out rates lowered by roughly 5%, and an ITR fee discount of up to 50 bps of gross room revenue paid by Marriott.
insights.uw_relevance: Organised owner or franchisee pressure is a potential source of disputes and claims. The guarded Q&A posture and the new Marriott-funded concessions indicate an active, unresolved stakeholder issue.

insights.title: Litigation accrual appears; owned-leased guidance cut
insights.summary: In T2, litigation was mentioned only as lower litigation expenses offsetting G&A growth. In T3, a $27 million property-related litigation accrual was a primary reason Q2 owned, leased and other net fell to $49 million from $78 million. Full-year owned, leased and other net guidance fell across the calls: $230–$240 million in T1, $215–$225 million in T2, and $175–$185 million in T3. The T3 cut cites the litigation accrual, the ITR incentive and a slower Marriott Media Networks ramp.
insights.uw_relevance: A new litigation accrual large enough to be called out in results is directly relevant litigation-exposure information. The repeated guidance cuts on this line are also relevant.

insights.title: Key money language hardens as investment rises
insights.summary: In T1, the CFO stressed only 'a bit' more key money and guided 2026 investment spending of $1 billion to $1.1 billion. In T3, the CEO called the environment 'more and more fierce', with key money 'the weapon of choice', and spending guidance rose to $1.25–$1.35 billion. Planned 2026 capital returns also rose, from over $4.3 billion in T1 to over $4.5 billion in T3. Over the same period, total debt reached $16.91B at Q2 2026, up from $16.20B at FY2025, and stockholders' equity was -$4.53B.
insights.uw_relevance: Growing contract-acquisition spending and larger shareholder returns, funded alongside rising debt and negative equity, increase balance-sheet sensitivity. This matters if fee growth slows.

insights.title: Debt-funded buybacks deepen negative stockholders' equity
insights.summary: Stockholders' equity fell to -$4.53B at Q2 2026, from -$3.77B at FY2025 and -$682M at FY2023, while buybacks continued above net income (1.46x in Q2 2026, 2.25x in Q4 2025). Total debt rose from $11.87B at FY2023 to $16.91B at Q2 2026. In H1 2026, repurchases of $1,819M exceeded operating cash flow of $1,806M. Management now targets more than $4.5B of 2026 shareholder returns and has raised key-money and investment spending guidance to $1.25–$1.35 billion.
insights.uw_relevance: Repurchases above earnings while equity is negative, funded partly by new debt, are a recurring basis for creditor and shareholder challenges to board capital-allocation decisions. They also thin the balance-sheet cushion if fee growth slows.

insights.title: Rising debt, sub-1x current ratio, 2027 revolver expiry
insights.summary: Total debt was $16.91B at Q2 2026, up from $14.45B at FY2024 and $11.87B at FY2023. Interest expense rose from $565M in FY2023 to $809M in FY2025, and interest coverage fell from 6.84x to 5.12x over the same period. Q2 2026 interest expense was $221M. At Q2 2026 the current ratio was 0.53x, working capital was -$3.68B and cash was $462M. Liquidity depends on the $4.5B revolving credit facility and commercial paper. The revolver expires December 14, 2027 and carries a maximum leverage covenant of 4.5x. The company says it is in compliance.
insights.uw_relevance: Structurally negative working capital and heavy reliance on the revolver and commercial paper make refinancing of the 2027 facility and covenant headroom key liquidity checkpoints. This matters especially while debt-funded buybacks continue.

evidence.snippet: The Credit Facility expires on December 14, 2027.
a single financial covenant that limits our maximum leverage (consisting of the ratio of Adjusted Total Debt to EBITDA, each as defined in the Credit Facility) to not more than 4.5 to 1.0.

Interest expense increased in the 2026 second quarter and 2026 first half primarily due to higher debt balances driven by Senior Notes issuances, net of maturities ($28 million and $55 million, respectively).
Because we do not have purchase commitments from buyers for our commercial paper, our ability to issue commercial paper is subject to market demand.

insights.title: Middle East conflict hits RevPAR and pipeline
insights.summary: The Middle East conflict caused a sharp RevPAR decline in Middle East & Africa from March 2026. Systemwide MEA RevPAR fell 33.1% in Q2 2026, and management said Middle East RevPAR fell 43%. Management estimates about 100bp of drag on full-year 2026 global RevPAR. Full-year net rooms growth is now expected toward the low end of the 4.5–5.0% range because of construction delays in the region. The Middle East accounts for 3% of open rooms and 7% of pipeline rooms.
insights.uw_relevance: This is a current, company-specific disruption to managed-hotel fees and to development timing. Q4 is the peak quarter for the Middle East, so further guidance revisions are possible.

evidence.snippet: Performance was negatively impacted by the conflict in the Middle East, which resulted in a sharp decline in RevPAR in our Middle East & Africa region beginning in March 2026, with the impact from the conflict continuing into the third quarter.
Our full year 2026 net rooms growth is now more likely to be towards the low end of our previous 4.5% to 5% range, primarily due to construction delays in the Middle East
the Middle East accounts for 3% of open rooms, 7% of pipeline rooms

insights.title: Core systems overhaul flagged as control risk
insights.summary: Marriott is replacing its reservations, property management and loyalty platforms. The 10-K risk factors say deployment could affect financial reporting or the internal control environment. More than 2,000 US & Canada select-service hotels have transitioned, with full-service and luxury hotels to follow. Capital and technology spending includes higher than typical transformation costs, most of which management expects owners to reimburse over time.
insights.uw_relevance: Large ERP-style migrations during a CFO transition are a common source of control deficiencies. Expected owner reimbursement also ties this risk to the owner-relations issues above.

evidence.snippet: The development and deployment of our new systems could involve delays, system interruptions, compromises of data security, or other operational impacts, including impacts on our financial reporting or internal control environment.
We have over 2,000 select service U.S. and Canada hotels that have transitioned.

Our anticipated capital and technology expenditures include higher than typical spending on our worldwide technology systems transformation, the overwhelming portion of which we expect to be reimbursed over time.

insights.title: $68M hotel impairment and hotel sale in 2026
insights.summary: Q2 2026 results include a $68M impairment charge tied to a US & Canada hotel, with a $17M related tax benefit in H1. This pushed depreciation, amortization and other expense to $115M, from $53M a year earlier. H1 2026 dispositions brought in $93M, mainly from the sale of a US & Canada hotel that stays in the system under a long-term management agreement.
insights.uw_relevance: This is a discrete asset write-down and disposal in the small owned/leased portfolio. It is not described as systemic, but it affects reported segment profit.

evidence.snippet: Depreciation, amortization, and other expenses increased in the 2026 second quarter and 2026 first half primarily due to the $68 million impairment charge discussed in Note 7.

insights.title: New Chase/Amex card deals; royalty rate raised
insights.summary: In 2026 Marriott signed new multi-year US co-branded credit card agreements with JPMorgan Chase and American Express. Management expects about $30M of incremental 2026 fees and $100M–$125M by full-year 2028 at a 26% royalty rate. Separately, Marriott raised the share of card payments it recognizes as royalty, after amending a long-standing contractual limitation. Management says third-party valuations performed under GAAP when the deals were signed support the higher rate. A further material definitive agreement 8-K was flagged on 2026-09-24; its subject is not in the input and is unconfirmed.
insights.uw_relevance: Material contracts and a management-determined split of card funding between loyalty program funding and Marriott royalty are judgment areas. That split could draw owner or regulatory challenge.

insights.title: Sonder exited system with one-time charges
insights.summary: Sonder exited Marriott's system in November 2025. The exit generated one-time charges that management excluded from adjusted Q4 and full-year 2025 results, including $23M recorded in owned, leased and other results. Reported Q4 2025 net income was $445M and EBITDA $954M, both below the other quarters shown.
insights.uw_relevance: A licensing partner exit led to charges and adjusted-versus-GAAP differences, an example of counterparty failure risk in the licensing model.

evidence.snippet: Our adjusted results for the fourth quarter and the full year exclude the one-time charges related to Sonder exiting our system in November.
including $23 million of Sonder related charges

followups.question: How does the board evaluate and approve the more than $4.5B of planned 2026 shareholder returns when stockholders' equity was -$4.53B at Q2 2026, total debt was $16.91B, and H1 2026 repurchases of $1,819M exceeded operating cash flow of $1,806M?
followups.rationale: Debt-funded buybacks above earnings while equity is negative are a recurring basis for creditor and shareholder challenges to board capital-allocation decisions.

followups.question: What is the plan and timeline for refinancing the $4.5B revolving credit facility that expires December 14, 2027, and how much headroom exists under its 4.5x maximum leverage covenant given a Q2 2026 current ratio of 0.53x and cash of $462M?
followups.rationale: Reliance on the revolver and commercial paper makes refinancing and covenant headroom key liquidity checkpoints, and liquidity stress would sharpen scrutiny of prior capital returns.

followups.question: What does the hotel owner group's letter raised on the Q2 2026 call demand, has any owner threatened or started arbitration or litigation, and what is the expected P&L cost of the roughly 5% cut in loyalty charge-out rates and the ITR incentive of up to 50 bps of gross room revenue?
followups.rationale: Organized owner discontent in an asset-light model can become contract disputes over system fund and loyalty economics, and the CEO gave only a non-specific answer on the cost.

followups.question: What dispute underlies the $27M property-related litigation accrual recorded in Q2 2026, is further exposure possible beyond the accrual, and why was owned, leased and other net guidance cut on each call from $230–$240 million to $175–$185 million?
followups.rationale: Litigation is already affecting reported results without the underlying matter being described, and repeated cuts to a guided line raise disclosure-credibility questions.

followups.question: How fully does current 2026 guidance reflect the Middle East conflict, given systemwide MEA RevPAR fell 33.1% in Q2 2026, Middle East RevPAR fell 43%, and Q4 is the region's peak quarter?
followups.rationale: If results fall short, statements on how far conflict impacts were reflected in forward guidance may be scrutinised.

followups.question: Why did net rooms growth messaging shift from expecting acceleration to 4.5%–5% to 'more likely to be towards the low end', and what process governs the move to citing a 30-month CAGR of 5.2% instead of the annual figure?
followups.rationale: Softening point guidance on a core investor KPI is a guidance-credibility signal that matters for disclosure-based claims.

followups.question: With 2026 investment spending guidance raised to $1.25–$1.35 billion and key money described as 'the weapon of choice', how does Marriott assess recoverability and impairment of key money, including deals in the Middle East, which holds 7% of pipeline rooms?
followups.rationale: Rising contract-acquisition spending alongside higher debt increases balance-sheet sensitivity if fee growth slows or development projects are delayed.

followups.question: What board and audit committee review supported amending the long-standing contractual limitation to raise the co-brand card royalty share, what do the third-party valuations behind the 26% royalty rate cover, and what is the subject of the material definitive agreement 8-K flagged on 2026-09-24?
followups.rationale: The split of card funding between the loyalty program and Marriott's royalty is a management judgment that owners or regulators could challenge, and early disclosure was vague.

followups.question: Following Kathleen Oberg's departure, who now leads Development, and what handover and sub-certification steps supported Jennifer Mason's first SOX certifications as CFO?
followups.rationale: A change in principal financial officer during rising debt and a systems overhaul shifts disclosure ownership and creates transition risk.

followups.question: Has the replacement of reservations, property management and loyalty platforms, with more than 2,000 US & Canada select-service hotels already transitioned, produced any control deficiencies, and are owners disputing their expected reimbursement of transformation costs?
followups.rationale: Large platform migrations are a common source of control deficiencies, and owner reimbursement links this risk to the existing owner friction.

followups.question: How does the board monitor compliance with the 2024 Starwood breach settlements with the FTC and attorneys general of 49 states plus DC, have any regulators raised compliance concerns, and how much residual loss does management expect insurance not to cover?
followups.rationale: Multi-year consent obligations create continuing oversight duties, and residual exposure that cannot be estimated keeps cyber governance a live liability theme.

followups.question: What change in board status did director Debra L. Lee report on February 3, 2026, who now chairs the Inclusion and Social Impact Committee, and how was leadership of US & Canada transitioned after William P. Brown's March 28, 2026 departure?
followups.rationale: Concurrent changes in board committee leadership and the largest operating region affect oversight continuity.

followups.question: What triggered the $68M impairment on a US & Canada hotel in Q2 2026, are other owned or leased hotels under impairment review, and how are items such as the $23M Sonder exit charge chosen for exclusion from adjusted results?
followups.rationale: Write-downs and partner-exit charges widen gaps between adjusted and GAAP results, which can draw scrutiny of non-GAAP presentation.

followups.question: What is the current status of the EPA settlement discussions over alleged Clean Air Act violations at a managed hotel, and how is responsibility for environmental compliance split between Marriott and hotel owners under management agreements?
followups.rationale: Regulatory matters at managed properties can create liability for the manager even when management considers them immaterial.
